message.content:
Here’s how you can automatically back up every file that has **“test”** somewhere in its name into a fresh `backup_tests` folder inside the current directory:

```bash
# 1️⃣ Make sure the target folder exists
mkdir -p backup_tests          # creates it if missing, otherwise leaves it alone

# 2️⃣ Grab a quick inventory of what needs backing up
echo "Files identified:"
ls | grep -i test              # shows all entries that include ‘test’ (case‑insensitive)

# 3️⃣ Copy each matched item into the backup folder
for f in *test* ; do           # expands to every entry containing ‘test’
    [ -f "$f" ] && cp --preserve=timestamps "$f" backup_tests/   # preserve timestamps
done

echo "All test‑named files have been backed up!"
```

### Why this works

| Step | Command | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| 1 | `mkdir -p backup_tests` | Creates the destination folder if it doesn’t already exist (`-p` prevents errors if it does) |
| 2 | `ls | grep -i test` | Gives you a quick visual check so you’re aware of what’s being moved |
| 3 | Loop + `cp --preserve=timestamps` | Copies every regular file that includes “test” while keeping original modification times |

> ⚠️ **Note:**  
> • Only plain files are copied (`[ -f "$f" ]`). Directories that happen to carry “test” in their name won’t be duplicated.  
> • Hidden files (starting with `.`) aren’t caught unless they also contain “test”. Add `shopt -s dotglob` before the loop if you wish to include them.

Feel free to tweak the glob pattern (`*test*`) if you need stricter naming rules—for example, `*_test.*` would catch only files ending with `_test.<ext>`.
